author: A Robot
objectives: Students will determine the steric number of a central atom from its Lewis structure by counting bonding pairs and lone pairs.
Students will predict the electron-domain geometry of a molecule from its steric number, identifying the linear, trigonal planar, tetrahedral, trigonal bipyramidal, or octahedral arrangement.
Students will distinguish electron-domain geometry from molecular geometry, and identify the molecular shape produced when one or more domains is a lone pair.
Students will explain why lone pairs occupy more angular space than bonding pairs, and predict the direction of bond-angle deviations from idealized values.
Students will apply VSEPR predictions to specific molecules and compare predicted geometries to experimentally observed structures.

modules.description: Introduces the core principle of VSEPR: electron domains around a central atom repel one another and arrange to minimize repulsion. Students see a central atom and learn to count domains from a Lewis structure.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Understand the fundamental principle of VSEPR theory: electron pair repulsion drives geometry.
Learn to count bonding and lone pairs from a Lewis structure.
Recognize that VSEPR predicts 3D geometry from 2D Lewis structures.
instructions: Watch the narration as the central atom and reference Lewis structure appear.
Pay attention to how electron domains are counted from the flat Lewis structure.
Note the core idea: repulsion minimizes by spacing domains apart.

H₂O Lewis Structure

VSEPR: Electron pairs repel.

clips.changeMeaning: Scene initializes with the title and central atom appearing. This establishes the starting point for learning VSEPR.
clips.narration: Welcome to VSEPR Theory. In this lab, we'll discover how to predict the three-dimensional shape of molecules.

clips.changeMeaning: Lewis structure panel appears alongside the central atom, establishing the connection between flat Lewis structures and 3D geometry. This teaches students how to identify electron domains.
clips.narration: VSEPR stands for Valence Shell Electron Pair Repulsion theory. The central idea is simple: electron pairs in bonding regions and lone pairs around a central atom repel one another. To minimize repulsion, these electron domains spread as far apart in space as possible.

clips.changeMeaning: Principle label appears to reinforce the concept. Now students understand how to count domains and the fundamental driving force behind molecular geometry.
clips.narration: To apply VSEPR, we count electron domains around the central atom. Each single bond, double bond, triple bond, or lone pair counts as exactly one domain. So water has four domains: two bonding pairs—one for each O-H bond—and two lone pairs on the oxygen. We call this the steric number.

modules.description: Demonstrates the minimum-repulsion principle by adding electron domains one at a time. Students watch 2, 3, and 4 domains arrange themselves into linear, trigonal planar, and tetrahedral geometries.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Predict and name the electron-domain geometry for steric numbers 2, 3, and 4.
Understand the characteristic angles and symmetry of linear, trigonal planar, and tetrahedral arrangements.
Connect the repulsion principle to the final arranged geometry.
instructions: Observe as domains are added one at a time.
Watch the domains move and settle into their minimum-repulsion configuration.
Note the angles and geometry name for each configuration.

components.text: Linear: 180°

clips.changeMeaning: Two domains appear at arbitrary positions, then animate toward opposite sides of the central atom, settling into the linear geometry. The geometry label appears confirming 'Linear: 180°'.
clips.narration: Let's start with two electron domains around a central atom. They repel each other, so they move as far apart as possible. The result is a linear arrangement, with domains pointing in opposite directions, 180 degrees apart.

clips.changeMeaning: A third domain appears and all three animate into the trigonal planar arrangement. The geometry label updates to show 'Trigonal Planar: 120°'.
clips.narration: Now we add a third domain. The three domains rearrange themselves. Two can't be 180 degrees apart anymore because there's a third. The three settle into a trigonal planar geometry: equally spaced around the central atom, 120 degrees apart in a flat plane.

clips.changeMeaning: A fourth domain appears and all four animate into tetrahedral positions. The label updates to 'Tetrahedral: 109.5°', showing the characteristic angle of this highly symmetric arrangement.
clips.narration: Add a fourth domain. The four arrange themselves into a tetrahedral geometry: one domain points to each corner of an imaginary tetrahedron. The angle between any two domains is approximately 109.5 degrees. This is the most common geometry for molecules in organic chemistry.

modules.description: Completes the catalog of electron-domain geometries by demonstrating trigonal bipyramidal (5 domains) and octahedral (6 domains) arrangements. Includes a summary panel showing all five geometries with their characteristic angles.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Predict and name the electron-domain geometry for steric numbers 5 and 6.
Understand the equatorial/axial distinction in trigonal bipyramidal geometry.
Recognize the complete set of five fundamental electron-domain geometries and their angles.
Relate geometry to steric number.
instructions: Observe the rearrangement as the fifth and sixth domains are added.
Notice the equatorial and axial positions in the trigonal bipyramidal geometry.
Study the summary panel showing all five geometries for reference.

components.text: Trigonal Bipyramidal: 3 Equatorial @ 120°, 2 Axial @ 90°

Five Electron-Domain Geometries
2 domains: Linear (180°)
3 domains: Trigonal Planar (120°)
4 domains: Tetrahedral (109.5°)
5 domains: Trigonal Bipyramidal (90°/120°)
6 domains: Octahedral (90°)

clips.changeMeaning: Five domains appear and animate into trigonal bipyramidal positions. Three are colored to indicate equatorial placement; two are different to show axial positioning. The label confirms the geometry and characteristic angles.
clips.narration: Now add a fifth domain. The geometry becomes trigonal bipyramidal. Three domains arrange in a plane around the central atom at 120 degrees, called the equatorial plane. Two additional domains point above and below, along the axial direction, at 90 degrees to the equatorial plane. This arrangement minimizes repulsion for five domains.

clips.changeMeaning: A sixth domain appears; all six rearrange into octahedral positions. The geometry label updates to show 'Octahedral: 90°'. This completes the set of five fundamental electron-domain geometries.
clips.narration: Finally, a sixth domain. All six arrange themselves into an octahedral geometry: one domain points to each face of an octahedron. All neighboring domains are 90 degrees apart. The octahedral geometry is common in transition metal complexes and some main-group molecules.

clips.changeMeaning: The summary panel appears, listing all five geometries with their steric numbers and characteristic angles. This provides a reference and reinforces the complete catalog.
clips.narration: We have now seen all five electron-domain geometries. Each corresponds to a different steric number: two domains give linear, three give trigonal planar, four give tetrahedral, five give trigonal bipyramidal, and six give octahedral. Each geometry places electron domains as far apart as possible for that steric number.

modules.description: Demonstrates the distinction between electron-domain geometry (arrangement of all electron pairs) and molecular geometry (shape of atoms only). Shows how replacing bonding pairs with lone pairs changes the molecular shape while keeping electron-domain geometry constant.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Distinguish between electron-domain geometry and molecular geometry.
Recognize that lone pairs occupy positions in the electron-domain geometry but do not define the molecular shape.
Predict how replacing bonding pairs with lone pairs changes molecular shape.
Name molecular geometries: tetrahedral, trigonal pyramidal, bent.
instructions: Observe the tetrahedral arrangement with three bonding domains and no lone pairs (methane).
Watch as bonding domains are replaced with lone pairs one at a time.
Notice how the electron-domain geometry stays tetrahedral but the molecular shape changes.
Read the labels identifying both geometries at each stage.

components.text: H
H
H
H

CH₄ (Methane)
Electron-domain: Tetrahedral
Molecular: Tetrahedral

NH₃ (Ammonia)
Electron-domain: Tetrahedral
Molecular: Trigonal Pyramidal

H₂O (Water)
Electron-domain: Tetrahedral
Molecular: Bent

clips.changeMeaning: Four hydrogen atoms appear bonded to the central atom in tetrahedral positions. The label shows methane with both geometries identified as tetrahedral.
clips.narration: Let's examine methane, CH₄. The central carbon atom has four bonding pairs—one with each hydrogen. All four domains are bonding pairs, so they arrange into a tetrahedral geometry. Since all four corners of the tetrahedron are occupied by atoms, we say the molecular geometry is also tetrahedral. Electron-domain geometry and molecular geometry are the same.

clips.changeMeaning: One hydrogen disappears and a lone pair cloud appears in its place. The label updates to show that the electron-domain geometry remains tetrahedral but the molecular geometry is now trigonal pyramidal.
clips.narration: Now replace one of the hydrogen atoms with a lone pair. This is ammonia, NH₃. The central nitrogen still has four electron domains around it—three bonding pairs and one lone pair. The electron-domain geometry is still tetrahedral. But the lone pair is invisible in the shape we draw; only the three atoms matter. When we trace the positions of the atoms alone, we see a triangular pyramid—trigonal pyramidal geometry. The electron-domain geometry and molecular geometry are different!

clips.changeMeaning: A second hydrogen disappears and a second lone pair appears. The label updates to show water: electron-domain geometry tetrahedral, molecular geometry bent.
clips.narration: Replace a second hydrogen with a lone pair. This is water, H₂O. The central oxygen now has four electron domains—two bonding pairs and two lone pairs. The electron-domain geometry remains tetrahedral because there are still four domains. But only two atoms are bonded to the oxygen. Tracing the two hydrogens alone, we trace a bent shape. Water has tetrahedral electron-domain geometry but bent molecular geometry.

modules.moduleName: Lone Pair Angular Asymmetry & Bond Angles
modules.description: Explains why lone pairs occupy more angular space than bonding pairs and examines how bond angles deviate from idealized values. Compares methane (109.5°), ammonia (107°), and water (104.5°).
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Explain why lone pairs occupy more angular space than bonding pairs.
Predict how bond angles deviate when lone pairs are present.
Calculate approximate bond angles in molecules with lone pairs.
Understand the connection between lone pair repulsion and reduced bond angles.
instructions: Observe the three molecules side by side: methane, ammonia, water.
Compare the sizes of the lone-pair clouds to the bonding domains.
Note the labeled bond angles for each molecule.
Optionally toggle the overlay view to see all three molecules superimposed.

components.text:
Lone pairs are repelled by only one nucleus.
Bonding pairs are repelled from two nuclei.
Lone pairs occupy more angular space, pushing bonding pairs closer.

clips.changeMeaning: All three molecules appear in the scene side by side. Methane is shown with four bonds at the ideal tetrahedral angle of 109.5°.
clips.narration: In methane, CH₄, all four electron domains are bonding pairs shared between the central carbon and hydrogen atoms. The ideal tetrahedral angle is 109.5 degrees. Since there are no lone pairs, the actual bond angles in methane are exactly 109.5 degrees.

clips.changeMeaning: The lone pair in ammonia is rendered larger than the bonding domains to visually convey that it occupies more space. The bond angle updates to 107°, showing the reduction from the ideal value.
clips.narration: In ammonia, NH₃, one of the four electron domains is a lone pair. The lone pair is not bonded to an atom on the other end; it is held only by the nitrogen nucleus. This means it is not pulled away from the nitrogen by another attraction. The lone pair therefore spreads out more in space, occupying a larger angular region. It repels the three bonding pairs more strongly, pushing them together. The H-N-H bond angle in ammonia is reduced to about 107 degrees—smaller than the ideal 109.5 degrees.

clips.changeMeaning: The two lone pairs in water are rendered even larger than in ammonia. The bond angle updates to 104.5°. The explanation panel appears, summarizing the principle of lone pair angular asymmetry.
clips.narration: In water, H₂O, there are two lone pairs around the central oxygen. Both are held by only the oxygen nucleus, so both spread out more than bonding pairs. The two lone pairs together repel the two bonding pairs very strongly. As a result, the H-O-H bond angle in water is compressed to about 104.5 degrees—even smaller than in ammonia. This is why water's H-O-H angle is noticeably smaller than the tetrahedral ideal of 109.5 degrees.

clips.changeMeaning: All eight molecules appear in the scene arranged in two rows: the top row shows molecules with all-bonding domains (CO₂, BF₃, CH₄, PF₅, SF₆); the bottom row shows molecules with lone pairs (NH₃, H₂O, XeF₄). This provides a comprehensive visual reference.
clips.narration: Now let's see VSEPR theory applied to real molecules. We'll look at examples spanning all five electron-domain geometries, and several where lone pairs modify the shape. For each molecule, we show the Lewis structure and the 3D geometry, and confirm how many bonding pairs and lone pairs are around the central atom.

clips.changeMeaning: The first three molecules are highlighted in sequence, with labels confirming their steric numbers and geometries.
clips.narration: On the left, we have CO₂, carbon dioxide. The central carbon forms two double bonds with oxygen atoms. Two electron domains, no lone pairs: linear geometry at 180 degrees. Next, BF₃, boron trifluoride: three bonding domains, no lone pairs—trigonal planar, 120 degrees. Then CH₄, methane: four bonding domains—tetrahedral, 109.5 degrees.

clips.changeMeaning: PF₅ and SF₆ are highlighted, showing the characteristic arrangements of trigonal bipyramidal and octahedral geometries.
clips.narration: Moving to the larger geometries: PF₅, phosphorus pentafluoride, has five bonding domains—trigonal bipyramidal, with three equatorial fluorines at 120 degrees and two axial fluorines at 90 degrees. Finally, SF₆, sulfur hexafluoride, has six bonding domains—octahedral, with all fluorines at 90-degree angles.

clips.changeMeaning: The lone-pair-containing molecules (NH₃, H₂O, XeF₄) are highlighted with their labels updated to show both electron-domain and molecular geometries.
clips.narration: In the lower row, we see how lone pairs modify molecular geometry. Ammonia, NH₃, has a tetrahedral electron-domain geometry but only three atoms bonded—trigonal pyramidal shape. Water, H₂O, has four electron domains but two are lone pairs—the molecular shape is bent. XeF₄, xenon tetrafluoride, has six electron domains with two lone pairs occupying the axial positions—the four fluorines form a square planar arrangement.

components.text: VSEPR Theory: Five Key Concepts

1. Minimum-Repulsion Principle

Electron pairs repel one another and arrange to be as far apart as possible.

2. Five Electron-Domain Geometries

Linear (2), Trigonal Planar (3), Tetrahedral (4), Trigonal Bipyramidal (5), Octahedral (6)

3. Electron-Domain vs. Molecular Geometry

Electron-domain = all pairs. Molecular = atoms only. Lone pairs invisible in shape.

4. Lone Pair Angular Asymmetry

Lone pairs occupy more space than bonding pairs, reducing bond angles.

5. Application to Real Molecules

Apply VSEPR to predict and confirm geometries of CO₂, BF₃, CH₄, PF₅, SF₆, NH₃, H₂O, XeF₄, and more.

You now understand VSEPR theory: the principle, the five geometries, how to distinguish electron-domain from molecular geometry, why lone pairs matter, and how to apply these ideas to predict molecular shapes.

clips.changeMeaning: The recap title appears at the top of the scene, signaling the start of the summary.
clips.narration: You've completed the VSEPR lab. Let's review the five key concepts that form the foundation of molecular geometry.

clips.changeMeaning: All five concept panels appear, one by one, and the closing statement emphasizes the integrated understanding. Students now have a complete mental model of VSEPR theory.
clips.narration: First, the minimum-repulsion principle: electron pairs repel, and molecules adopt geometries that place them as far apart as possible. Second, the five electron-domain geometries: linear, trigonal planar, tetrahedral, trigonal bipyramidal, and octahedral, each with characteristic angles. Third, the distinction between electron-domain geometry—the arrangement of all electron pairs—and molecular geometry—the shape traced by atoms alone. Fourth, lone pair angular asymmetry: lone pairs occupy more space than bonding pairs, reducing bond angles below idealized values. And fifth, the application: using these principles to predict and confirm the structures of real molecules. Together, these ideas let us predict how any covalent molecule arranges itself in three dimensions.
